sec.title: Background
sec.p: Inflammation is associated with an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD). Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory drug that can be used to improve clinical outcomes in patients with CAD.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL up to August 2025 to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that reported clinical outcomes with the use of colchicine in CAD. Data for outcomes was extracted and summary estimates were generated using a random effects model.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 16 RCTs were included reporting data for 20,601 patients. The pooled analysis demonstrated a non-significant difference between colchicine and control groups for reducing all-cause death (RR: 0.97; 95 % CI, 0.78–1.22), cardiovascular death (RR: 0.98; 95 % CI, 0.79–1.21), and stroke (RR: 0.67; 95 % CI, 0.39–1.15). However, colchicine significantly reduced the risk of myocardial infarction (RR: 0.74; 95 % CI, 0.59–0.93), and ischemia-driven revascularization (RR = 0.72; 95 % CI, 0.53–0.99) at the expense of an increased risk of gastrointestinal adverse events (RR = 1.83; 95 % CI, 1.38–2.43) as compared to control.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Colchicine does not reduce the relative risk of all-cause and cardiovascular death in patients with CAD. However, it can reduce the risk of myocardial infarction and ischemia drive revascularization. Additional trial data are required to confirm these findings.
Keywords: Colchicine, Inflammation, Coronary artery disease, meta-analysis
Received 2025 Sep 5; Accepted 2025 Sep 9; Collection date 2025 Nov.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a major global health burden [1,2], remaining the primary cause of death and disability despite tremendous advances in medical therapies and interventional strategies. Although treatments such as antiplatelet agents, statins, and revascularization procedures have improved outcomes, residual cardiovascular risk remains, greatly enhanced by underlying inflammation that promotes atherosclerosis progression and plaque destabilization [3,4].

Traditionally, colchicine has been used as an anti-inflammatory drug in the management of gout and pericarditis [5]. Recent interest in its possible role in cardiovascular disease is premised on its ability to potently inhibit several major pathways mediating inflammation, notably by disrupting two key inflammatory pathways: the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 signaling [6]. This has been supported by earlier clinical trials, including the COLCOT [7] and LoDoCo2 [8], which demonstrated decreases in major adverse cardiovascular events, such as myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and cardiovascular mortality among patients with both stable and post-MI CAD.

Although meta-analyses have been conducted to determine the efficacy of colchicine in CAD in past, their results were mainly driven by small trials with low statistical power [[9], [10], [11]]. However, recent evidence has come from the CLEAR trial [12]; which is the largest randomized study on this subject with more than 7000 patients. Hence, it is important to update the current literature with such significant new data. Thus, this updated meta-analysis was conducted to provide a comprehensive review of the use of colchicine in reducing cardiovascular risk and to inform future clinical practice on CAD management. Moreover, we conducted subgroup analyses stratified by acute and chronic CAD, duration of therapy, and drug dosages to further evaluate the role of colchicine.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: This meta-analysis was undertaken following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines [13,14]. This meta-analysis does not include any patient collected/investigated directly by the authors, so formal ethical approval was not necessary. The protocol of review has been registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024616009).

sec.title: Data sources and searches
sec.p: We searched the following databases and registered trials from inception till August 2025: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase. A combination of specific keywords and medical subject headings (MeSH), including “Colchicine,” “Acute coronary syndrome,” “ coronary artery disease”, “CAD” and “RCT,” was employed (Table S1: Search strategy). Boolean operators (AND, OR) were applied to combine terms and optimize retrieval of relevant studies.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria and outcomes
sec.p: The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Study design: RCTs; (2) Population: Patients with acute or chronic CAD; (3) Intervention: Colchicine; (4) Comparator: placebo or standard treatment; (5) Outcome: reporting at least one outcome of interest. The primary outcomes were all-cause death and cardiovascular death. The secondary outcomes included stroke, myocardial infarction, gastrointestinal adverse effects, ischemia driven revascularization and treatment discontinuation/withdrawal. The definitions for the reporting criteria used to assess gastrointestinal adverse effects are outlined in Table S2: Definitions used.

sec.title: Selection process
sec.p: We used Rayyan to manage the screening and deduplication of studies retrieved from our online search. After eliminating duplicates, two authors independently reviewed the titles and abstracts of the remaining studies. Subsequently, a detailed full-text evaluation was conducted by the same authors. Any disagreements arising during the process were resolved by consultation with a third author.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: Data on study characteristics, including authors, study locations, intervention (colchicine dose and intended treatment duration), sample sizes, follow-up durations, and demographic information (mean age, sex ratio), as well as clinical parameters such as comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension, smoking) and background medication usage (beta-blockers, statins, aspirin and/or clopidogrel), were extracted. Information on prior cardiac interventions, including PCI, MI, and CABG, was also recorded. These data were organized into a pre-piloted Excel sheet.

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: The quality evaluation of all included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted utilizing the Cochrane “Risk of Bias” tool (RoB 2.0) [15]. Each included study was assessed for bias and categorized as having either low, high, or some concerns.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: All data analysis was performed in R version 4.4.1 using the ‘meta’ package. Risk Ratios (RR) with corresponding 95 % confidence intervals (CI) were pooled. The DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model was utilized to accommodate the variability observed among the studies. To assess the degree of statistical heterogeneity among the included trials, the I2 statistic was employed. For analyses involving more than 10 studies, publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot. Egger's test was applied to evaluate funnel plot asymmetry. To explore the high heterogeneity, leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were conducted, where each study was sequentially removed to determine its influence on aggregate findings. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the type of coronary artery disease (acute versus chronic CAD), the duration of colchicine therapy (≤30 days versus >30 days), and the dosage of colchicine (>0.5 mg/day versus single-dose or ≤0.5 mg/day). A p-value <0.05 indicated statistical significance.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: The initial search yielded 1113 articles. After removing 427 duplicate records, 686 records remained for screening based on their titles and abstracts. Out of these, 610records were excluded, leaving 76 reports selected for full-text assessment. No reports were excluded during the retrieval phase. Ultimately, 16 studies were included in the final review. The details for study inclusion process are provided in PRISMA flowchart Fig. 1.

caption.p: PRISMA flowchart depicting the screening and study selection process.

sec.title: Study characteristics
sec.p: The 16 included trials enrolled a total of 20,601 patients (colchicine: 10,351 patients, control: 10,250 patients) with a median follow-up duration ranging from 1 month to 2.5 years. Colchicine dosing varied, with 0.5 mg being the commonest dosing regimen, while other studies utilized higher doses or loading doses depending on the clinical setting. The mean age of participants ranged from 56 to 67 years, and most studies included a predominantly male population (52 %–93.7 %). Smoking status was inconsistently reported, with current or prior smoking ranging from 3.5 % to 71.7 % among the trials. The prevalence of comorbidities, follow-up duration, and baseline LVEF% were variably reported by the trials. The detailed study characteristics are highlighted in Table 1.

sec.title: Risk of bias
sec.p: Fourteen studies had an overall low risk of bias. Two studies had some concerns of bias, mainly due to missing outcome data and deviations from intended interventions [16,17]. The details of the bias assessment for each included study are shown in the Fig. S1.

sec.title: All-cause death
sec.p: Twelve RCTs with a total of 20,409 patients reported all-cause death. The pooled analysis demonstrated that the risk of all-cause death was comparable between the two groups (RR, 0.97; 95 % CI, 0.78–1.22; P = 0.82; I2 = 17 %) (Fig. 2A). Subgroup analyses did not demonstrate any significant findings when stratified by acute versus chronic CAD (Pinteraction = 0.41), short- versus long-term colchicine administration (Pinteraction = 0.41), or lower- versus higher-dose colchicine dosage regimens (Pinteraction = 0.46) (Figs. S2–S4). There was no evidence of publication bias on the inspection of funnel plot asymmetry (Egger's test, P = 0.9) (Fig. S5).

caption.p: Forest plots of A) All-cause death, (B) Cardiovascular death, (C) Myocardial infarction.

sec.title: Cardiovascular death
sec.p: Twelve RCTs with a total of 19,805 patients reported cardiovascular death. The pooled analysis demonstrated no statistically significant difference between the two groups (RR, 0.98; 95 % CI, 0.79–1.21; P = 0.86; I2 = 0 %) (Fig. 2B). No significant subgroup differences were observed based on acute versus chronic CAD (Pinteraction, 0.37), short- versus long-term colchicine administration (Pinteraction, 0.99) or lower- versus higher-dose colchicine dosage (Pinteraction, 1.00) (Figs. S6–S8).

sec.title: Myocardial infarction
sec.p: A pooled analysis of nine RCTs (19,529 patients) demonstrated a significantly reduced risk of MI in the colchicine group as compared to placebo (RR, 0.74; 95 % CI, 0.59–0.93; P < 0.01). The analysis showed moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 32 %) (Fig. 2C). Subgroup analyses based on chronic versus acute CAD (Pinteraction, 0.16), duration of colchicine therapy (Pinteraction, 0.41), and colchicine dosage (Pinteraction, 0.75) did not reveal any significant findings (Figs. S9–S11).

sec.title: Stroke
sec.p: A pooled analysis of nine RCTs involving 19,838 patients evaluated the incidence of stroke and found no statistically significant difference between the colchicine and placebo groups (RR = 0.67; 95 % CI, 0.39–1.15; P < 0.14) (Fig. 3A). The analysis showed moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 38 %). Subgroup analyses based on acute versus chronic CAD (Pinteraction, 0.88), duration of colchicine therapy (Pinteraction, 0.22), and colchicine dosage (Pinteraction, 0.88) did not reveal any significant findings (Figs. S12–S14).

caption.p: Forest plots for (A) Stroke, and (B) Ischemia driven revascularization,

sec.title: Ischemia-driven revascularization
sec.p: Six RCTs with a total of 18,746 patients reported on revascularization rates. The pooled showed that colchicine administration was associated with a lower risk of ischemia driven revascularization procedures (RR = 0.72; 95 % CI, 0.53–0.99; P = 0.04) (Fig. 3B). The heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 63 %). Subgroup analyses based on acute versus chronic CAD (Pinteraction, 0.51), and colchicine dosage (Pinteraction, 0.88) did not reveal any significant findings (Figs. S15–S16).

sec.title: Gastrointestinal adverse effects
sec.p: Fifteen RCTs involving 20,379 patients reported GI adverse effects, which comprised of diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain. The pooled analysis showed that colchicine administration was associated with a higher risk of gastrointestinal adverse effects as compared to placebo (RR = 1.83; 95 % CI, 1.38–2.43; P < 0.01) (Fig. 4A). The analysis showed substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 77 %). Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis did not reveal any significant findings (Fig. S17). The test for interaction was significant based on short- versus long-term colchicine therapy (Pinteraction, 0.02) as well as lower- versus higher-dose colchicine treatment (Pinteraction = 0.02) (Figs. S18–S19). Subgroup analysis based on acute versus chronic CAD did not reveal any significant findings (Pinteraction, 0.39) (Fig. S20). Asymmetry was noted in the funnel plot (Egger's test, P = 0.001) (Fig. S21).

caption.p: Forest plots for (A) Gastrointestinal adverse events and (D) Discontinuation/withdrawal.

sec.title: Treatment discontinuation/withdrawal
sec.p: Twelve RCTs (12,731 patients) reported about treatment discontinuation. The pooled analysis showed that the risk for treatment discontinuation was significantly higher in the colchicine group as compared to placebo (RR = 1.48; 95 % CI, 1.08–2.03; P = 0.02) (Fig. 4B). The analysis showed significant heterogeneity (I2 = 70 %). Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis did not reveal any significant findings (Fig. S22). The test for interaction was significant based on lower- versus higher-dose colchicine treatment (Pinteraction, 0.03) (Fig. S23). Subgroup analyses based on acute versus chronic CAD (Pinteraction, 0.43), and duration of colchicine therapy (Pinteraction, 0.48) did not reveal any significant findings (Figs. S24–S25). Asymmetry was noted in the funnel plot (Egger's test, P = 0.01) (Fig. S26).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This meta-analysis based on 20,601 patients found that colchicine resulted in a significant reduction of the risk of MI and ischemia-driven revascularization in patients with CAD, with no effect on all-cause or cardiovascular mortality. Additionally, gastrointestinal side effects were more common with colchicine as compared to the control group.

Our results demonstrate no significant reduction in all-cause or cardiovascular mortality with colchicine. This is an important finding as it suggests that while colchicine has beneficial effects on certain ischemic endpoints, it does not confer a survival benefit in CAD patients. The lack of a mortality benefit across both acute and chronic CAD populations and varying durations and dosages of colchicine use suggests that its anti-inflammatory effects, while sufficient to reduce ischemic events, may not address the broader systemic complications of CAD that contribute to mortality [18,19]. For clinicians, this underscores the importance of prioritizing proven strategies for reducing mortality. This includes implementing optimal medical therapy with statins, antiplatelets, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi), rather than solely relying on colchicine to mitigate mortality risk [20].

Both the current and previous reviews confirm that colchicine significantly reduces the risk of MI. This finding is clinically relevant, especially for patients with a high residual risk of recurrent ischemic events despite guideline-directed medical therapy. Colchicine's ability to reduce MI may be attributed to its role in attenuating neutrophil activation and suppressing inflammasome signaling pathways involved in plaque instability [21]. In the setting of secondary prevention, where recurrent MI is one of the major causes of morbidity, the addition of colchicine to conventional treatment may offer additional protection, especially in high-risk populations. Additionally, the absence of significant subgroup interactions for MI prevention across acute versus chronic CAD and different dosages or treatment durations suggests that colchicine's MI-reducing effects are consistent across various patient groups. This further strengthens its potential role as an adjunctive therapy in a broad CAD population.

Interestingly, while the prior meta-analyses demonstrated a significant reduction in stroke with colchicine, our updated meta-analysis did not find a statistically significant difference. This difference may be attributed to variations in study populations or the inclusion of more recent data, such as the CLEAR trial, which could have diminished the stroke-reduction effect seen in prior analyses. This suggests that although inflammation plays a role in both coronary and cerebrovascular events, the inflammatory pathways targeted by colchicine may be more pertinent to coronary atherosclerosis than stroke pathophysiology. Given the differing etiologies and embolic risks associated with ischemic stroke, particularly in patients with atrial fibrillation or CAD, colchicine may have a limited role in cerebrovascular event prevention. Hence, clinicians should continue to rely on anticoagulation and optimal carotid revascularization strategies for stroke prevention in CAD patients.

Colchicine significantly reduced the rates of ischemia-driven revascularizations. This benefit likely comes from stabilizing vulnerable plaques and hence it can reduce the need for subsequent percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI) or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Colchicine is a useful addition to consider in patients having recurrent symptoms of ischemia and those undergoing PCI, especially if there is suspicion of plaque instability. Decreasing the frequency of revascularization events may also improve long-term outcomes and save healthcare costs [22].

Colchicine increases the incidence of gastrointestinal side effects, which include diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal discomfort. Our updated analysis, however, provides more specific findings regarding this adverse event profile with significant subgroup interactions based on colchicine dose and duration. These effects were more pronounced in patients receiving higher doses and those receiving long-term colchicine therapy; in fact, significant subgroup interactions suggest a dose and duration-dependent relationship. Additionally, colchicine's gastrointestinal effects are expected due to its mechanism as an anti-tubulin agent, which disrupts microtubules, affecting mitosis and cell replication [23,24]. Cells with high turnover, like those in the gastrointestinal tract, are particularly vulnerable to its effects. For clinicians, it reiterates the importance of proper patient selection and dosing when considering colchicine for CAD as colchicine is known to have a narrow therapeutic index, with effective plasma concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 3 ng/ml, and toxicity occurring above 3 ng/ml [25]. Lower doses or shorter treatment durations may mitigate the risk of gastrointestinal intolerance, although this must be balanced against the need for adequate anti-inflammatory dosing to achieve clinical efficacy. Additionally, the marked increase in treatment discontinuation rates in the colchicine group emphasizes the clinical significance of these gastrointestinal side effects. The practical consequence of gastrointestinal intolerance may be a failure to continue treatment, reducing the potential cardiovascular benefit. Treatment should therefore be started with close monitoring and education of the patient, and alternatives should be considered for the patients unable to tolerate colchicine.

In summary, our updated meta-analysis confirms most of the benefits and risks previously associated with colchicine in CAD, while providing new insights. The findings from this meta-analysis indicate colchicine can be an adjunctive therapy useful in CAD, specifically in reducing the risk for MI and ischemia-driven revascularization. However, its lack of significant impact on mortality and stroke, coupled with the high incidence rates of gastrointestinal adverse effects and discontinuation of treatment, lead to the conclusion that colchicine should not be considered as a replacement for standard treatments, but rather as an adjunct in carefully selected patients. For clinicians, the key to maximizing colchicine's utility lies in patient selection, dose optimization, and close monitoring for adverse effects, ensuring that its anti-inflammatory benefits are harnessed without compromising patient adherence or tolerability. Further research is needed to explore the long-term effects of colchicine in different CAD populations, including its role in primary prevention and patients with comorbid conditions such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease. More data is also needed to establish the mechanisms that explain its differential impacts on coronary versus cerebrovascular events.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This meta-analysis has some limitations. First, for outcomes such as gastrointestinal side effects and treatment discontinuation, there was moderate to substantial heterogeneity that may reflect differences in study designs, colchicine dosing, and patient populations. While our subgroup analyses explored some of these differences, they may still overlook other potential confounding factors such as comorbidities, concomitant medications, and the intensity of background therapies, which were not uniformly reported across trials. Variability in study protocols, as well as potential biases (e.g., differences in blinding and follow-up duration), could also affect results, particularly for subjective outcomes like gastrointestinal adverse effects and treatment discontinuation. A key limitation of our analysis is that the included trials did not consistently report distinctions between fatal and non-fatal MI, nor did they systematically detail the specific causes of non-CV death. Consequently, our findings are restricted to total MI and all-cause mortality as defined in the original studies. While colchicine appears to reduce MI and revascularization without affecting all-cause or CV mortality, it remains unclear whether its benefit is confined primarily to non-lethal events or whether any offsetting increase in non-CV causes of death exists. Future RCTs and patient-level data meta-analyses are needed to clarify these distinctions and provide a more precise understanding of colchicine's impact on fatal versus non-fatal outcomes.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Colchicine causes a significant reduction in MI and ischemia-driven revascularization events in patients with CAD; however, it does not affect all-cause and cardiovascular death. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more pronounced in patients receiving higher doses or longer durations of colchicine treatment.
